paras: The threatened lynching of Jasper Hays took place at Sandfly Station, near Savannah, Georgia, on the morning of August 5, 1900, when an armed crowd of street railway men hunting the killer of a motorman held Hays, a Black man first named as the shooter, at gunpoint. Some of the men wanted to punish him on the spot, but he convinced them that his brother Seaborn had fired the shots, and he was handed to a patrolman and jailed. His brother was later arrested by officers and convicted of murder, while the Black Savannah Tribune condemned the armed gathering as an unlawful mob.

On the night of Saturday, August 4, white passengers on an Isle of Hope car of the Savannah, Thunderbolt and Isle of Hope road ejected two Black men who had been quarreling in foul language, putting them off about a mile from Sandfly Station. When the car returned to the station, a man stepped in front of it, ordered motorman Lucius B. Varnadoe to halt and fired; Varnadoe fired back, and the gunman escaped. The Savannah Morning News first named the gunman as Jasper Hays, and Varnadoe died at the Savannah Hospital the next evening.

Early on Sunday, about twenty or twenty-five of Varnadoe's fellow motormen and conductors took a special car to the scene and searched the area. When Jasper Hays came up to the station, the men covered him with pistols, guns and rifles and ordered him to throw up his hands. According to the Morning News, "Some of the crowd were for dealing him summary punishment at once," until he explained that his brother Seabrook, or Seaborn, was the man they wanted.

The crowd then brought Jasper into Savannah and made him lead them to his brother's haunts. At daylight they turned him and a woman named McKeever over to Patrolman Tom Murphy, who had been aiding the search, and both were jailed. The next day the paper wrote that the men had gone out "with the purpose of making short work of Hays should he be captured" and that talk of a "lynching bee" was current in the city.

The railway offered a $100 reward, and two more brothers, Joseph and Jim Hays, were arrested. On August 11 a posse led by Police Sergeant Henry W. Baughn arrested Seaborn Hayes at Josh Butler's house on the Ogeechee road, where he said Varnadoe had shot first. A grand jury indicted him and two companions, Joseph Lloyd and James Blige, as principals, and Butler and Edward Gardner as accessories after the fact.

At trial the defense argued that Varnadoe, whose dying statement named Jasper, had fired first. The jury found Seaborn Hayes guilty on August 17, and he was sentenced to hang on September 28. A motion for a new trial followed, and on September 12 the judge granted a supersedeas suspending the execution. No report of Jasper Hays's release, or of any action against the men who held him, appears in the coverage.

The Savannah Morning News, the only white paper found to cover the case, headlined its first story "NEGRO PUTS TWO BULLETS INTO" the motorman and called Seaborn Hays "the murderer" from the second day. It reported the lynching talk with little disapproval, remarking that if Hays were taken soon the county might only have to pay for a coffin and a coroner's jury. Its arrest story dismissed Hayes's self-defense claim as one that "Will Hardly Bear Investigation".

The Savannah Tribune, a Black weekly, answered on August 11 with an editorial, "An Unfortunate Affair," that called the shooting cowardly and regretted by Black citizens. It singled out the armed gathering meant to "lynch" the accused, wrote that "The gathering of such mobs are wholly unlawful," and asked that the accused be tried and, if guilty, legally punished. A week later its Port Royal column argued that Hayes had more provocation than the killer of a Black man named Stewart and that the conductor, not the passengers, should have dealt with him.
Passengers and Varnadoe's dying statement had the gunman firing first, while the Hays brothers said the motorman fired first; the jury accepted the prosecution's version.

reader.title: Threatened lynching of Jasper Hays
bases: An armed crowd of 20-25 street railway men hunting the accused shooter held Jasper Hays at gunpoint, some wanting 'summary punishment', and the papers reported their purpose was to make 'short work' of Seaborn Hays and talk of lynching him (A2, A3, A5).
No one was killed by the crowd: Jasper Hays was released into police custody after explaining he was not the shooter, and Seaborn Hayes was later arrested by officers and tried in court (A2, A6, A9).
The Savannah Morning News (A2, A3) and the Black Savannah Tribune (A5) both report an armed gathering at the scene intent on seizing and lynching the accused.

accounts.label: Passengers' and motorman's account
accounts.gist: Hays lay in wait at Sandfly Station, ordered the car to halt and fired first; Varnadoe returned fire only after two shots.

accounts.label: Seaborn Hayes's account
accounts.gist: Varnadoe shot at him twice first and he fired in self-defense, as Jasper said his brother told him that night and as Hayes said after his arrest.

accounts.label: Morning News on the armed crowd
accounts.gist: Varnadoe's co-workers went out armed to search; some wanted summary punishment for Jasper, and they meant to make 'short work' of Seaborn if captured.

accounts.label: Black editorial
accounts.gist: The shooting was cowardly and regretted by Black citizens, but the armed gathering to arrest and lynch the accused was unlawful and should not have been allowed without deputization.

framing.detail: The Savannah Morning News headlined 'NEGRO PUTS TWO BULLETS INTO' the motorman, called Seaborn Hays 'the murderer' before trial, and reported the 'lynching bee' talk with a jest about the county paying only for a coffin, while later stressing due process.
It dismissed Hayes's self-defense claim in a headline as a story that 'Will Hardly Bear Investigation'.
The Savannah Tribune's 'An Unfortunate Affair' condemned the shooting and the armed mob alike and asked for a lawful trial.
The Tribune's Port Royal Notes said Hayes had more provocation than the killer of a Black man named Stewart and blamed the conductor.

conflicts.note: The first report and Varnadoe's dying statement named Jasper; from Aug. 6 the Morning News, the grand jury and the trial named Seaborn, and the defense argued the motorman had confused the brothers (A9).
The jury accepted the prosecution's version (A9); the self-defense version comes from Hayes and his brother.
Spelling varies across issues; the place is printed Sandfly Station.

record_check.dossier: Jasper Hays was the man the crowd held at gunpoint; Seaborn Hays was the accused shooter the crowd sought but never reached, later arrested by officers and tried.
threatened: the crowd held Jasper at gunpoint and some called for summary punishment, but no attempt on his life is reported.
About 20-25 motormen and conductors of the Savannah, Thunderbolt and Isle of Hope road, Varnadoe's companions.

info: Shooting of the motorman on Saturday night, Aug. 4, 1900; the armed crowd went to Sandfly Station and held Jasper Hays early Sunday morning, Aug. 5.
Sandfly Station on the Savannah, Thunderbolt and Isle of Hope railway, near Savannah; the search continued in Savannah (Perry street lane, Gordon street lane).
Jasper Hays, Black ('negro'), held at gunpoint by the crowd; the person the crowd sought, his brother Seaborn (Seabrook) Hays, was never reached by it.
Jasper Hays was first reported as the man who shot motorman Lucius B. Varnadoe; the accusation was shifted the next day to his brother Seaborn Hays.
Motormen and conductors of the street railway, companions and friends of Varnadoe, who went out on a special car.
Seaborn Hayes found guilty of murder and sentenced to hang Sept. 28; a new-trial motion was filed and a supersedeas suspended the execution. No report of Jasper Hays's release was found.
